title: Double the box
concept: Doubling length, width and height of a box multiplies its surface (paint) by 2x2 = 4 and its volume (water) by 2x2x2 = 8.
kept: The student's question: paint and water for a box made twice as long, wide and tall
Guess first, then build the small box, then the big box
Build from little cubes and count the squares on the outside
Lego-like look: bright bricks with studs on a green baseplate
Their answer (area x4, volume x8) is correct and is what the counts show
filled_in: Concrete size: small box 3 long, 2 wide, 2 tall (a cube would hide which doubling matters); big box 6 x 4 x 4
One guess with four combined options (both x2, paint x8/water x4, paint x4/water x8, both x4), including the 'double is double' idea
Build by adding one layer at a time; paint button covers every outside face including the bottom
Units: 1 cube = 1 cup of water, 1 outside square = 1 patch of paint (labelled as a model)
Two short 'why' steps (paint x4, water x8) with a per-side square count table
A slider to multiply every side by 1 to 4, with a computed table, as the exploring step
math_check: All numbers are counted in code from the cube list: cubes = cells in the layers built, squares = cube faces with no neighbouring cube. Small 3x2x2: 12 cubes, 32 squares (top+bottom 12, front+back 12, left+right 8). Big 6x4x4: 96 cubes, 128 squares. Ratios 96/12 = 8 and 128/32 = 4. For factor k the code gives k^2 paint and k^3 water (k=3: 324 cubes and 288 squares, which is 27x and 9x). The 'why' text numbers use the box dimensions and the counted per-side totals. check-page passed with no problems or warnings at desktop and phone width.
